kicker: Lesson 15 of your course, built from Chapter 15 of your Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology textbook (Rizzo). Test practice uses checked answers, because there is no official key for this test.

steps.title: What the lymphatic system does
teach: The lymphatic system works alongside the blood. It moves a fluid called lymph through its own vessels, returns it to the blood, and helps destroy microorganisms.

Its primary function is to drain protein-containing fluid that escapes from blood capillaries out of the tissue spaces. It also carries fats from the digestive tract to the blood, produces lymphocytes and develops immunity.

act.prompt: What is the primary function of the lymphatic system?

options.label: Draining protein-containing fluid that escapes from blood capillaries

steps.title: From plasma to lymph
teach: Blood pressure pushes some plasma out of capillaries into the spaces between cells, where it’s called interstitial fluid. Most is reabsorbed, but the rest must be drained or swelling (edema) develops.
Once interstitial fluid enters a lymphatic capillary, it’s called lymph: mostly water with ions, gases, nutrients, some proteins, hormones, enzymes and wastes.
In the small intestine, special lymphatic vessels called lacteals absorb fats. The milky, fat-filled lymph there is chyle.

act.prompt: Put the fluid’s names in order.

steps.title: Lymphatic vessels
teach: Lymphatic capillaries start as blind-ended tubes between cells. They’re much larger and more permeable than blood capillaries. They’re absent from the central nervous system, red marrow and some other tissues.
They join into lymphatics, which look like veins but have thinner walls and more valves, so lymph flows one way.
Lymphatics of the skin run in loose subcutaneous tissue and follow the veins; lymphatics of the organs follow the arteries.
Lymph keeps moving thanks to skeletal muscle contractions, breathing movements and smooth muscle in the vessel walls. A blockage causes edema; in elephantiasis, parasitic worms block the vessels.

steps.title: Lymph nodes
teach: Lymph nodes (lymph glands) are oval or bean-shaped structures along the lymphatics, 1 to 25 mm long. They cluster in three regions: the groin, armpits and neck.

Afferent lymphatic vessels enter a node at several points. Efferent vessels leave at the hilum, the dent on one side. A fibrous capsule sends trabeculae inward, creating compartments with lymph nodules (with germinal centers that make lymphocytes) and sinuses lined with macrophages.
When lymph enters, microbes trigger lymphocyte production, and macrophages clean up by phagocytosis. Swollen nodes usually mean an infection.

mnemonic.explanation: Afferent vessels bring lymph into the node; efferent vessels carry it out.

steps.title: Lymphatic trunks and ducts
teach: Efferent vessels unite into six principal lymphatic trunks: lumbar (legs, pelvis, kidneys), intestinal (stomach, intestines, pancreas, spleen), bronchomediastinal (thorax, lungs, heart, diaphragm and part of the liver), intercostal (part of the thorax), subclavian (arms) and jugular (head and neck).

The trunks drain into two ducts. The thoracic duct (left lymphatic duct) is the main collecting duct and empties into the left subclavian vein. The right lymphatic duct empties into the right subclavian vein. That returns lymph to the blood.

steps.title: Tonsils
teach: Tonsils are masses of lymphoid tissue in mucous membrane, forming a protective ring around the nose and mouth.

The palatine tonsils, at the back of the mouth, are the ones commonly removed in a tonsillectomy. The pharyngeal tonsils (adenoids) are near the back of the nasal cavity. The lingual tonsils are on the back surface of the tongue at its base.

items.label: Near the back of the nasal cavity
At the base of the tongue

steps.title: Spleen, thymus, Peyer’s patches and appendix
teach: The spleen, in the upper left abdomen, is the single largest mass of lymphatic tissue. It filters blood, destroys bacteria and worn-out red cells and platelets, makes lymphocytes and stores blood as a reservoir.
The thymus is a two-lobed mass in the mediastinum along the trachea. It’s the site of lymphocyte production and maturation, especially T cells. It’s largest at puberty and then shrinks.
Peyer’s patches in the wall of the small intestine have macrophages that destroy bacteria. The appendix helps B cells mature and makes IgA.

items.label: Filters blood and destroys worn-out red cells

steps.title: B cells and T cells
teach: Immunity is the body’s ability to resist pathogens, foreign substances and harmful chemicals. The bulk of our lymphoid tissue is in the lymph nodes.

B lymphocytes produce antibodies and give humoral immunity, which works against circulating bacteria and viruses. B cells that enter tissue become plasma cells, which make huge amounts of one antibody.
T lymphocytes, from the thymus, give cellular immunity, effective against fungi, parasites, viruses inside cells, cancer cells and transplanted tissue.

steps.title: Antigens and antibodies
teach: Antigens are foreign proteins (on bacteria, viruses, protozoa or fungal spores). They trigger antibodies, or immunoglobulins: Y-shaped proteins of two heavy and two light chains, with antigen-binding sites at the tips. Binding makes invaders clump so phagocytes can eat them.

Five types: IgG (tissue fluid and plasma; attacks viruses, bacteria and toxins; activates complement), IgA (secretions like tears, saliva and breast milk), IgM (plasma; response to bacteria and food antigens), IgD (on B cells; B-cell activation) and IgE (allergic reactions).

mnemonic.explanation: The five immunoglobulins: G, A, M, E, D. IgE = allergies (think "E" for "eek, pollen!").

items.label: Attacks viruses, bacteria and toxins in plasma
In tears, saliva and breast milk
On the surface of B cells

steps.title: Active and passive immunity
teach: Active immunity: your own B cells make antibodies. Natural active: getting the infection. Artificial active: a vaccine with killed or weakened pathogens, which builds memory without the full illness.

Passive immunity: you receive someone else’s antibodies. Natural passive: antibodies cross the placenta to the fetus and last months. Artificial passive: gamma globulin, immune serum or antivenom; immediate but lasting only 2 to 3 weeks.

steps.title: Cells and chemicals of the immune response
teach: Macrophages engulf antigens and present them on their surface; T cells can only bind antigens presented this way.

Helper T cells stimulate killer T cells and more B cells. Killer T cells kill virus-invaded cells and cancer cells. Suppressor T cells slow the response once the infection is controlled. Memory cells are descendants of activated T and B cells from the first response; they last for years and speed up future responses.

Lymphokines from T cells include interleukin-2 (stimulates proliferation of T and B cells), gamma interferon and perforin. Macrophages release interleukin-1 (fever) and tumor necrosis factor. Complement proteins break down microbes.

items.label: Last for years after an infection
Stimulates T and B cell proliferation

steps.title: Lymphatic and immune disorders
teach: Lymphangitis is inflammation of lymphatic vessels with red streaks in the skin. Lymphadenitis is inflammation of lymph nodes. Lymphoma is a tumor of lymphatic tissue (Hodgkin’s and non-Hodgkin’s). Splenomegaly is an abnormal enlargement of the spleen, which can follow infections.

AIDS is caused by HIV infecting T lymphocytes. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic inflammatory disease with a red butterfly-shaped rash over the nose and cheeks. Allergies involve IgE; anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening reaction.
Bone marrow transplants are used to treat disorders such as leukemia, lymphomas and immune deficiencies.

items.label: Inflamed lymphatic vessels with red streaks
Butterfly rash over the nose and cheeks

steps.title: Immunity and aging
teach: The thymus shrinks and is replaced by fat, so fewer new T cells mature. T and B cells respond less, so older adults get more infections and more autoimmune problems. Vaccines and yearly flu shots are recommended. Latent viruses can reactivate, like chickenpox returning as shingles.

act.prompt: Why can shingles appear later in life?

options.label: Weaker immunity lets the latent chickenpox virus reactivate
A new infection with a different virus
options.feedback: It’s the same chickenpox virus reactivating.

quiz.q: Lymphatics of the ____________________________ travel in loose subcutaneous connective tissue and generally follow the routes of veins.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 15 says lymphatics of the skin travel in loose subcutaneous connective tissue and generally follow the routes of veins. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 15.

quiz.q: Lymphatic vessels that enter the lymph node at various sites are called _________________ lymphatic vessels.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 15 says lymphatic vessels that enter the lymph node at various sites are afferent lymphatic vessels. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 15.

quiz.q: The ______________ gland is a bilobed mass of tissue in the mediastinum along the trachea.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 15 says the thymus gland is a bilobed mass of tissue in the mediastinum along the trachea. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 15.

quiz.q: Inflammation of the lymphatic vessels with accompanying red streaks visible in the skin is called ____________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 15 says lymphangitis is an inflammation of the lymphatic vessels with red streaks visible in the skin. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 15.

quiz.q: Which structures are found in the walls of the small intestine where their macrophages destroy bacteria?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 15 says Peyer’s patches are in the wall of the small intestine and their macrophages destroy bacteria. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 15.

quiz.q: The ______________________ trunk drains the thorax, lungs, heart, diaphragm, and part of the liver.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 15 says the bronchomediastinal trunk drains the thorax, lungs, heart, diaphragm and the rest of the liver. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 15.

quiz.q: An abnormal enlargement of the spleen that can develop from infections is called _______________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Splenomegaly is the medical term for an abnormally enlarged spleen, which can follow infections. The other options don’t mean an enlarged spleen. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 15.

quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 15 says killer T cells kill virus-invaded body cells and cancerous body cells. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 15.

quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 15 says immunoglobulin G is found in tissue fluids and plasma and attacks viruses, bacteria and toxins. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 15.

quiz.q: The ________________ is the site for lymphocyte maturation.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 15 says the thymus is a site for lymphocyte production and maturation. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 15.

quiz.q: The ___________________ tonsils are located at the back surface of the tongue at its base.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 15 says the lingual tonsils are located on the back surface of the tongue at its base. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 15.
